stem: A pharmacy repeatedly partially fills a morphine Schedule II prescription for a patient documented as terminally ill. Which statements are consistent with the federal special partial-fill pathway? Select all that apply.
choices: Record the date and quantity supplied with each partial dispensing
Each partial fill must be traceable.
Document the patient's terminally ill status for use of the special pathway
The special status is material to the record.
Stop using this prescription for partial fills after the 60-day period from issue, unless it ended sooner
The special framework has a 60-day endpoint.
Treat the remaining morphine as an ordinary refill that may continue for six months
C-II remainders are not ordinary refills.
Use the 72-hour stock-shortage deadline as the only governing clock because morphine is Schedule II
The terminally ill pathway is a distinct rule.
steps: Apply per-partial records and the 60-day limit
core: Terminally ill morphine partial filling uses the special federal C-II pathway with status documentation, per-dispensing records, and a 60-day endpoint.
facts: Discontinuation can end the prescription sooner.
trap: Defaulting to the familiar 72-hour C-II remainder rule.
distinct: Repeated real-opioid record task, not stock-short or patient-request partial filling.
anti_guess: All five options use authentic C-II partial-fill concepts.

stem: A practitioner sees a patient on August 14 and considers issuing separate future Schedule II prescriptions. Which sets are consistent with the federal multiple-prescription framework, assuming legitimate medical purpose and state law are satisfied? Select all that apply.
choices: Three methylphenidate prescriptions all dated August 14, totaling 90 days, with appropriate earliest-fill instructions on the later prescriptions
That structure can fit the federal pathway.
Three lisdexamfetamine prescriptions all issued on August 14, totaling 90 days, with later prescriptions carrying earliest-fill dates
Separate C-II prescriptions may be staged this way.
Two oxycodone prescriptions dated August 14 totaling 60 days, with the second carrying a lawful earliest-fill instruction
Federal multiple-prescription structure is not limited to stimulants.
Three methylphenidate prescriptions postdated September, October, and November even though all were actually issued August 14
Later prescriptions should not be postdated.
One oxycodone prescription written with five refills to create the same 90-day result
C-II refills remain prohibited.
steps: Confirm each drug is Schedule II
Check issue date, total supply, and earliest-fill instructions
core: Lawful future C-II therapy uses separate prescriptions issued on the real date with earliest-fill instructions; it does not use postdating or refills.
facts: The federal total under this pathway may not exceed a 90-day supply.
trap: Thinking the rule applies only to ADHD stimulants or permits postdating.
distinct: Multi-drug issuance matrix distinct from individual C-II validity questions.
anti_guess: Every option contains a C-II drug; document structure decides correctness.

stem: Each scenario involves methadone. Which statements correctly reflect how indication changes the federal pharmacy pathway? Select all that apply.
choices: A valid methadone prescription for pain can be evaluated under ordinary Schedule II prescription rules, subject to applicable state law
Pain use is not the OTP-maintenance pathway.
An ordinary community-pharmacy prescription written solely for ongoing OUD maintenance cannot be treated as routine Schedule II pain prescribing outside the applicable narcotic-treatment pathway
OUD maintenance invokes the special federal framework.
A qualifying non-OTP emergency provision is a narrow dispense-only bridge while referral is arranged
That emergency pathway differs from routine prescribing.
Methadone becomes Schedule III whenever the diagnosis is OUD
Indication does not reclassify methadone.
A pain prescription automatically becomes invalid if the patient also has a history of OUD
The actual medical purpose and facts must be evaluated.
steps: Apply ordinary C-II or narcotic-treatment pathway accordingly
core: Methadone remains Schedule II, but the legal dispensing pathway changes materially between pain and OUD maintenance treatment.
facts: The narrow non-OTP emergency provision is not ordinary retail prescribing.
trap: Using drug identity alone and ignoring medical purpose.
distinct: Same-drug indication matrix; Q0015 addresses pain quantity only.
anti_guess: Every choice concerns methadone, so schedule recognition alone is useless.

stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy receives an ordinary outpatient methadone prescription whose stated purpose is ongoing OUD maintenance. The prescriber is not operating through the applicable OTP pathway. What is the best response?
choices: Fill it as an ordinary Schedule II prescription because methadone prescriptions are identical regardless of indication.
OUD maintenance has a special federal pathway.
Recognize that routine retail prescribing is not the ordinary federal methadone-OUD maintenance pathway and do not process it as a standard pain prescription.
Indication changes the legal framework.
Add five refills so treatment is not interrupted.
C-II refills are prohibited.
Reclassify methadone to Schedule III for this patient.
The drug remains Schedule II.
Sell an equivalent OTC methadone product instead.
There is no such OTC substitution pathway.
steps: Identify methadone and OUD maintenance purpose
core: An ordinary community-pharmacy methadone prescription for OUD maintenance cannot simply be processed as a standard Schedule II pain prescription.
facts: Methadone prescribed for pain is legally distinct from methadone dispensed for maintenance treatment.
trap: Ignoring indication because the schedule is already known.
distinct: Direct pharmacist intake decision for OUD methadone.
anti_guess: All distractors keep methadone central rather than surrounding it with ordinary drugs.

stem: A non-OTP practitioner uses the narrow federal emergency provision while arranging OUD treatment referral and asks a pharmacy whether the rule authorizes a routine three-day methadone prescription. Which answer is correct?
choices: Yes; the rule is a three-day retail-prescription exception.
The federal exception is framed as emergency dispensing, not routine prescribing.

No; the pathway permits the practitioner to dispense no more than one day's medication at a time for no more than three days while referral is arranged, and it is not a renewable retail prescription rule.
That states the narrow emergency provision.
Yes; any community pharmacy may create the prescription after receiving a telephone request.
The pharmacy cannot create prescriber authority.
No; even emergency dispensing is never permitted outside an OTP.
The regulation contains the narrow emergency exception.
Yes; the practitioner may write 30 days and mark only the first three days 'emergency.'
That evades rather than follows the limit.
core: The federal three-day rule is a narrow practitioner-dispensing bridge, not authority for a routine three-day methadone retail prescription.
facts: The emergency period is used while referral for treatment is arranged.
trap: Remembering 'three days' but forgetting who dispenses and how.
distinct: Mechanism-focused methadone emergency question, not emergency C-II prescription law.
anti_guess: Every answer uses the same three-day context but changes the legal mechanism.

stem: Which statements correctly distinguish common federal OUD medication pathways? Select all that apply.
choices: A qualifying buprenorphine Schedule III prescription for OUD can use the ordinary prescription-dispensing framework when all current prescribing requirements are met
Schedule III-V narcotic treatment can have a prescription pathway.
Buprenorphine-naloxone remains Schedule III; the naloxone component does not make the product noncontrolled
The combination remains controlled.
Methadone for ongoing OUD maintenance is not handled as an ordinary community-pharmacy Schedule II pain prescription outside the applicable narcotic-treatment framework
Methadone maintenance is specially regulated.
Methadone and buprenorphine are legally interchangeable simply because both can treat OUD
Their schedules and treatment pathways differ.
Buprenorphine becomes Schedule VI in Massachusetts when used for OUD
Indication does not remove federal Schedule III status.
steps: Distinguish Schedule III prescription pathway from Schedule II methadone maintenance
Apply product status without indication-based reclassification
core: Buprenorphine products and methadone can both treat OUD but follow materially different controlled-substance treatment pathways.
facts: Massachusetts quantity limits are a separate issue from federal treatment authority.
trap: Treating all MOUD products as one legal class.
distinct: Pathway comparison rather than Q0006/Q0024 quantity questions.
anti_guess: All options concern recognized OUD medications and require product-specific law.

stem: Under current Massachusetts Policy 2024-05, which Schedule II/III prescriptions may qualify for up to a 90-day supply when otherwise lawful? Select all that apply.
choices: Methylphenidate for a non-opioid indication
Non-opioid S-II/III drugs can use the 90-day category.
Lisdexamfetamine for ADHD
This Schedule II stimulant is a non-opioid.
Testosterone cypionate replacement therapy
Testosterone is a non-opioid Schedule III example.
Buprenorphine for opioid use disorder
OUD treatment drugs are an express category.
Oxycodone for ordinary outpatient pain
Other S-II/III opioids remain subject to the 30-day maximum.
steps: Classify each drug as Schedule II/III
Identify OUD treatment or non-opioid category
core: Current Massachusetts policy allows up to 90 days for OUD drugs and non-opioid Schedule II/III drugs, while ordinary Schedule II/III opioids remain capped at 30 days.
facts: The policy also recognizes implantable infusion-pump prescriptions.
trap: Assuming every Schedule II drug shares the same Massachusetts quantity cap.
distinct: Five-drug independent classification burden beyond existing single-drug examples.
anti_guess: Four controlled drugs qualify for different reasons; one opioid pain drug is the near-miss.

stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy is preparing its next PMP Clearinghouse submission. Which dispensing transactions are generally included in the Schedule II-V/gabapentin reporting requirement? Select all that apply.
choices: Oxycodone
Schedule II dispensing is reportable.
Alprazolam
Schedule IV dispensing is reportable.
Pregabalin
Schedule V dispensing is reportable.
Gabapentin
Massachusetts specifically requires gabapentin reporting despite Schedule VI status.
Warfarin
Ordinary Schedule VI warfarin is not within the II-V/gabapentin reporting rule.
core: Massachusetts pharmacy reporting covers Schedule II-V dispensations plus gabapentin, a designated Schedule VI drug of concern.
facts: Covered transactions are reported within 24 hours or the next business day under current guidance.
trap: Either excluding gabapentin because it is Schedule VI or including every Schedule VI drug.
distinct: Ties the classification matrix directly to current submission action/deadline.
anti_guess: Four reportable drugs span II, IV, V, and the unique VI exception.

stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy submits naloxone dispensing information with its daily PMP data. How should the pharmacist understand that submission?
choices: It is collected for naloxone reporting purposes but does not appear on the patient's MassPAT profile.
Current guidance separates data collection from profile display.
Naloxone becomes federal Schedule II once it is submitted to the PMP.
Reporting does not change schedule.
The submission proves that all naloxone products require a prescription.
OTC and prescription naloxone are distinct products.
Naloxone must appear on the patient profile before the pharmacy may dispense another dose.
The data are not displayed that way.
PMP submission is prohibited because opioid antagonists may never be reported.
Massachusetts specifically requests naloxone dispensing data.
steps: Identify naloxone reporting as a separate data-collection requirement
Distinguish Clearinghouse submission from MassPAT profile display
core: Massachusetts collects naloxone dispensing data through the PMP mechanism, but those data do not appear on the patient's MassPAT profile.
facts: Patient ID collection is not required for naloxone dispensing data under current guidance.
trap: Assuming every item submitted to the PMP is displayed as controlled-prescription history.
distinct: Q0097/Q0098 address access and OTC/Rx product status, not PMP display.
anti_guess: Distractors connect reporting to plausible but incorrect schedule/access consequences.

stem: A Massachusetts practitioner has a valid professional license and MCSR authorizing Schedule VI activity but does not yet have a DEA registration. Which prescriptions are within that Schedule VI-only credential situation, assuming no other scope problem? Select all that apply.
choices: Warfarin
Warfarin is Massachusetts Schedule VI.
Insulin glargine
Insulin glargine is an ordinary Schedule VI prescription drug.
Gabapentin
Gabapentin is Massachusetts Schedule VI even though it is PMP-reportable.
Pregabalin
Pregabalin is federal Schedule V and requires DEA authority.
Methylphenidate
Methylphenidate is federal Schedule II and requires DEA authority.
steps: Separate Massachusetts Schedule VI from federal II-V
core: An MCSR-only practitioner can conduct approved Schedule VI activity, but federally controlled Schedules II-V require corresponding DEA registration.
facts: Gabapentin's PMP status does not make it federally controlled.
trap: Using MassPAT reporting as a proxy for DEA scheduling.
distinct: Real-drug credential matrix, not abstract registration recall.
anti_guess: Gabapentin is deliberately paired with Schedule V/II drugs to defeat PMP-based elimination.

stem: A Massachusetts practitioner with an appropriate MCSR but no DEA registration writes for gabapentin. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: The lack of a DEA registration does not by itself bar Schedule VI-only prescribing of gabapentin
Gabapentin is not federally scheduled.
The practitioner still needs the appropriate Massachusetts controlled-substance registration authority
Schedule VI remains controlled under Massachusetts law.
A pharmacy dispensing gabapentin generally submits the dispensing data to the Massachusetts PMP
Gabapentin is a designated reportable drug of concern.
PMP reporting automatically converts gabapentin to federal Schedule V
Reporting status does not change federal schedule.
The pharmacy must use the federal Schedule III/IV five-refills-in-six-months rule solely because gabapentin is reportable
PMP status does not import that federal refill rule.
steps: Separate state schedule, DEA status, and PMP status
core: Gabapentin combines Massachusetts Schedule VI/MCSR requirements with PMP reporting while remaining outside federal Schedules II-V.
facts: This mixed status is a common Massachusetts-specific exam trap.
trap: Letting one regulatory consequence imply every other controlled-substance consequence.
distinct: Consequence matrix for one drug rather than Q0122's basic classification distinction.
anti_guess: Same drug across every option requires separate legal classifications.

stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy is preparing multi-drug single-dose compliance packages. Which scenarios can fit the current policy's Schedule II/III maintenance-medication allowance, assuming all other requirements are satisfied? Select all that apply.
choices: Daily methylphenidate used as a stable maintenance medication
A Schedule II maintenance medication can fit the policy.
Stable testosterone cypionate therapy treated as a maintenance medication
Schedule III maintenance medication can fit.
Stable buprenorphine Schedule III maintenance therapy when otherwise compliant
The policy can include qualifying S-III maintenance medication.
A three-day acute oxycodone course added only because it is Schedule II
The policy's expansion is for maintenance medication, not every acute C-II course.
An alprazolam dose placed in the package without checking any other packaging/dispensing requirements solely because it is Schedule IV
The stated S-II/III maintenance expansion does not erase other requirements.
steps: Apply the compliance-packaging policy without erasing other rules
core: Current Massachusetts policy permits qualifying Schedule II/III maintenance medications in multi-drug single-dose packages; acute status and other packaging requirements still matter.
facts: The policy was revised to remove an older categorical exclusion of S-II/III maintenance medications.
trap: Interpreting 'Schedule II/III allowed' as a blanket controlled-drug exemption.
distinct: Real-drug maintenance matrix; no current bank packaging item.
anti_guess: Schedule and chronicity vary independently across plausible therapies.

stem: A patient receives a short acute oxycodone Schedule II course after dental surgery. The pharmacy notes that Massachusetts now allows Schedule II and III maintenance medications in multi-drug single-dose compliance packages. Does that policy statement alone justify adding this acute oxycodone course to the maintenance package?
choices: Yes, because every Schedule II medication is now automatically a compliance-packaging maintenance drug.
The policy is not a blanket S-II authorization.
No; the relevant expansion concerns Schedule II/III maintenance medications, so the acute nature of this course must not be ignored.
Maintenance status is the material fork.
Yes, because dental prescriptions are always treated as maintenance therapy.
Prescriber specialty does not create maintenance status.
No, because Schedule II drugs are still categorically prohibited from all compliance packaging.
That overstates the current policy.
Yes, but only if the pharmacy changes oxycodone to Schedule III on the label.
A pharmacy cannot reclassify the drug.
steps: Classify the course as acute rather than maintenance
core: The current policy's S-II/III expansion is tied to maintenance medications; an acute oxycodone course is not justified by schedule permission alone.
facts: Other patient-specific packaging requirements must also be satisfied.
trap: Remembering the newer permission but dropping the word 'maintenance.'
distinct: Acute-vs-maintenance pharmacist decision using a real C-II opioid.
anti_guess: Two opposite schedule-based shortcuts are both offered as distractors.

stem: It is August 14, 2026. A Massachusetts pharmacy is preparing to dispense isotretinoin. Which statements reflect the currently applicable FDA iPLEDGE situation on this date? Select all that apply.
choices: The pharmacy must participate in the iPLEDGE REMS/certified pharmacy pathway to dispense isotretinoin
Isotretinoin remains under iPLEDGE restricted distribution.
The patient must be enrolled and satisfy the applicable iPLEDGE requirements before dispensing
Patient enrollment/authorization remains part of the REMS.
The pharmacy should follow the currently implemented REMS rules rather than assume the February 2026 modifications already took effect
FDA delayed implementation to November 15, 2026.
The February 2026 modifications became fully effective on August 8, 2026 and must be treated as implemented today
FDA announced an implementation delay.
Isotretinoin became an ordinary unrestricted Schedule VI prescription when the implementation date changed
The delay did not remove the REMS.
steps: Fix the legal date at August 14, 2026
Distinguish approved modifications from their delayed implementation
core: Isotretinoin remains subject to current iPLEDGE requirements on August 14, 2026; FDA delayed the 2026 modifications until November 15, 2026.
facts: FDA continues to publish current iPLEDGE implementation updates.
trap: Confusing FDA approval of a REMS modification with its operational effective date.
distinct: Time-sensitive current REMS implementation task absent from the bank.
anti_guess: All options use real 2026 iPLEDGE events; timing, not product notoriety, decides.

stem: Which products currently require a product-specific restricted-distribution or certified-pharmacy REMS pathway before routine dispensing, based on the bank's current official-source verification? Select all that apply.
choices: Isotretinoin through iPLEDGE
iPLEDGE remains an active REMS.
Mifepristone under the Mifepristone REMS Program
Certified prescriber/pharmacy requirements remain current.
Sodium oxybate through its restricted REMS distribution system
Sodium oxybate remains subject to a restricted REMS.
Clozapine solely because the former Clozapine REMS still requires pharmacy enrollment
FDA removed the clozapine REMS requirement in 2025.
Warfarin through a certified-pharmacy restricted-distribution REMS
Warfarin does not have that restricted-distribution REMS.
steps: Account for the clozapine REMS removal
core: Current restricted-distribution REMS status differs across products and can change over time; isotretinoin, mifepristone, and sodium oxybate remain restricted while clozapine's former REMS does not.
facts: Product-specific REMS obligations must be checked against current FDA status.
trap: Remembering a historically famous REMS after FDA has removed it.
distinct: Cross-product current-status matrix; Q0106 and Q0109 are single-product items.
anti_guess: Three well-known restricted products compete with a formerly restricted product and a high-risk ordinary drug.

stem: A Massachusetts LTC facility has 120 licensed beds, so its Schedule II-V analgesic emergency-kit category is capped at 75 units. Which proposed analgesic configurations stay within that category cap? Select all that apply.
choices: 25 morphine units plus 25 oxycodone units
The total is 50 units.
40 morphine units plus 35 hydromorphone units
The total is exactly 75 units.
20 morphine, 20 oxycodone, and 20 hydromorphone units
The total is 60 units.
76 oxycodone units
That exceeds the 75-unit cap.
45 morphine units plus 31 oxycodone units
The 76-unit total exceeds the cap.
steps: Place the facility in the 101-150 bed tier
core: For 120 beds, the LTC analgesic category may contain up to 75 total approved Schedule II-V analgesic units, not 75 of each drug.
facts: The facility chooses its formulary with its pharmacy provider and need not stock the maximum.
trap: Applying the cap separately to each opioid rather than to the category total.
distinct: Real-drug aggregate-count decision rather than Q0149's single numerical recall.
anti_guess: Correct and incorrect configurations differ by small totals around the exact cap.

stem: A Massachusetts LTC facility has 120 licensed beds, giving its Schedule II-V sedative/anticonvulsant emergency-kit category a 25-unit cap. Which configurations stay within that cap? Select all that apply.
choices: 10 lorazepam units plus 10 alprazolam units
The category total is 20.
25 pregabalin units
That equals the 25-unit cap.
5 lorazepam, 5 alprazolam, and 5 pregabalin units
The total is 15.
26 lorazepam units
That exceeds the category cap.
15 alprazolam units plus 15 pregabalin units
The total is 30.
core: The LTC sedative/anticonvulsant cap is an aggregate category limit tied to licensed bed capacity.
facts: The corresponding analgesic cap for this bed tier is 75 units.
trap: Using the larger analgesic cap for sedatives or counting each drug separately.
distinct: Separate drug category and cap from Q0206 analgesics.
anti_guess: All options use plausible controlled sedative/anticonvulsant products and close totals.

stem: An inpatient Massachusetts hospice has 18 licensed beds. Under the acute-use ADD circular, its caps are 100 Schedule II-V analgesic units, 60 Schedule II-V sedative/anticonvulsant units, and 50 Schedule VI ancillary units. Which proposed category totals comply? Select all that apply.
choices: 100 units of approved morphine/other Schedule II-V analgesic stock in the analgesic category
That is at the 100-unit analgesic cap.
60 units of approved lorazepam/other Schedule II-V sedative stock in the sedative category
That is at the 60-unit cap.
40 units of an approved Schedule VI ancillary antiemetic in the ancillary category
That is below the 50-unit cap.
101 Schedule II-V analgesic units because one extra unit may be borrowed from the ancillary category
Category caps are separate.
70 Schedule II-V sedative units because the hospice has fewer than 21 beds
The 11-20 bed sedative cap is 60.
steps: Map each drug category to its separate cap
Reject shifting unused capacity across categories
core: Hospice acute-use limits are separate category caps; unused capacity in one category does not increase another category's limit.
facts: The hospice need not stock each maximum.
trap: Treating the three category maxima as one fungible pool.
distinct: Three-category hospice cap matrix rather than one-number recall.
anti_guess: All values cluster at or near the official limits.

stem: A Massachusetts inpatient hospice uses its acute-use ADD for morphine, lorazepam, and approved Schedule VI ancillary medications. Which actions fit the purpose and accountability of this program? Select all that apply.
choices: Use an acute morphine dose for timely palliation while the pharmacy prepares and delivers the patient's full prescription
That is the bridge-supply purpose.
Reconcile a lorazepam dose removed from the ADD with the patient's prescription/order
Dispensed ADD medication must be reconciled.
Keep the ADD contents as pharmacy property until doses are dispensed for administration
The pharmacy retains ownership until dispensing.
Use the cabinet to avoid filling routine long-term prescriptions whenever delivery is inconvenient
The program is not a substitute for routine pharmacy service.
Dispense untracked Schedule VI ancillary doses because they are outside federal Schedules II-V
Schedule VI stock remains subject to the program's controls.
steps: Apply pharmacy ownership and prescription reconciliation
core: Hospice acute-use ADD stock is a controlled bridge to full prescription delivery and remains pharmacy-owned and reconciled until dispensing.
facts: Each unit must be tamper-evident/resistant and individually packaged as a single dose.
trap: Treating palliative urgency as permission for undocumented floor stock.
distinct: Purpose/accountability pathway separate from Q0208 category limits.
anti_guess: Correct and incorrect scenarios all occur in realistic inpatient hospice operations.

stem: At an eligible Massachusetts hospital ADD, evaluate each stocking action independently. Which are permitted under the current technician stocking policy? Select all that apply.
choices: A PTT loads pharmacist-verified alprazolam with electronic validation under pharmacist direction/supervision
PTTs may stock verified Schedule III-VI.
A PTT loads pharmacist-verified methylphenidate because the pharmacist is available by phone
PTTs may not use this pathway for Schedule II.
A licensed non-PTT technician under pharmacist supervision loads pharmacist-verified methylphenidate with electronic validation
Licensed non-PTT technicians may stock verified Schedule II-VI.
A nationally certified licensed technician, without prior pharmacist verification, transfers sealed non-patient-specific warfarin using electronic validation
That fits the non-PMP Schedule VI shortcut.
A nationally certified licensed technician, without prior pharmacist verification, uses the same shortcut for gabapentin
PMP drugs such as gabapentin are excluded.
steps: Apply verification and supervision conditions independently
core: ADD stocking authority depends on the exact credential, schedule, verification status, and for the certified-tech shortcut, PMP status.
facts: Electronic validation is a common safeguard across these stocking pathways.
trap: Assuming 'technician' is one legal role or that national certification erases the gabapentin exclusion.
distinct: Capstone cross-credential matrix synthesizes three separate new ADD stocking pathways.
anti_guess: Every option is a close actor/drug pairing differing by one controlling fact.
